proof:
# Radius monotonicity and finite saturation of an ordinary central chord

## 1. Statement for three canonical lines

Use the six cyclic ray endpoints

    P_0=(A,0), P_1=(0,B), P_2=(-t,t),
    P_3=(-a,0), P_4=(0,-b), P_5=(r,-r),

and let R=(A,B,t,a,b,r). Let W_i>0 be the prescribed area in the sector between P_i and P_(i+1), with cyclic indices. Assume these endpoint/area data are realized by an actual planar convex body containing zero in its interior.

**Theorem.** Increase any one radius R_i to any value R_i' in the finite closed interval

    R_i<=R_i'<=min{2W_(i-1)/R_(i-1), 2W_i/R_(i+1)}.          (1)

Leave every other radius and every sector area fixed. The resulting data are again realized by a planar convex body containing zero in its interior. One may choose a polygon with at most 12 vertices. In particular the upper endpoint of (1) is attained and makes at least one adjacent sector exactly its core triangle.

Opposite radii R_i,R_(i+3) can be increased independently to their respective upper bounds. The corresponding central chord increases, while the other two central chords and all six sector areas remain fixed. If either radius actually increases, the normalized inverse weight of that chord strictly decreases.

The theorem changes the ordinary body. It does not preserve inter-fiber compatibility, unrelated support values, or cap depths in directions not determined by the three fixed lines.

## 2. Exact matrix proof

In these canonical coordinates every consecutive direction determinant and every next-neighbor direction determinant is one. The exact sector PSD criterion consequently has entries

    L_ii=1/(2W_(i-1))+1/(2W_i)-1/R_i^2,
    L_(i,i+1)=1/(2W_i)-1/(R_i R_(i+1)),                     (2)

and all other off-diagonal entries zero. Feasibility includes the core constraints

    R_i R_(i+1)<=2W_i.                                     (3)

These constraints make L a Z-matrix: every off-diagonal entry is nonpositive.

Increasing R_i changes only its diagonal entry and the two adjacent off-diagonal pairs. Every changed entry in (2) increases. Condition (1) is exactly what keeps the two affected inequalities (3) valid. Thus the new matrix L' is still a Z-matrix and satisfies L'>=L entrywise.

For every real vector x, write |x| for its coordinatewise absolute value. Then

    x^T L' x >= |x|^T L' |x|
                 >= |x|^T L |x| >=0.                       (4)

The first inequality uses the Z sign pattern. The second uses entrywise domination and nonnegativity of |x|. The last is the positive semidefiniteness of the original feasible matrix. Hence L' is positive semidefinite.

The exact PSD realization theorem now produces an actual convex polygon with the new endpoints and exactly the old sector areas. This proves feasibility at every point of the CLOSED interval (1), including its upper endpoint; no spectral gap or limiting body argument is required. All radii remain finite and positive. Its upper endpoint is at least the original radius by (3), and equality with one of the two bounds makes the corresponding sector area equal to its core area.

Opposite endpoints are not adjacent in the six-cycle. Their two sets of adjacent core constraints are disjoint, and neither endpoint appears as a neighbor in the other's bound in (1). They may therefore both be set to their respective bounds, in either order.

If the target chord length is ell and the other two normalized chord lengths are ell_2,ell_3, its inverse weight is

    1/[1+ell(1/ell_2+1/ell_3)].                              (5)

It strictly decreases when ell increases. Sector-area constraints, including cap fractions and sorted cap profiles, are preserved exactly.

## 3. Exact finite-data reduction for the target vertical chord

The target vertical chord has length B+b in the canonical coarea normalization. Its two finite upper endpoints are

    B'=min{2W_0/A, 2W_1/t},
    b'=min{2W_3/a, 2W_4/r}.                               (6)

After this operation at least one of W_0,W_1 is a core area and at least one of W_3,W_4 is a core area. Using the ordinary sector notation

    (W_0,W_1,W_2,W_3,W_4,W_5)
       =(Y_3,X_2,Y_1,X_3,Y_2,X_1),

the four possible pairs of saturated sectors are

    (Y_3,X_3), (Y_3,Y_2), (X_2,X_3), (X_2,Y_2).              (7)

Additional simultaneous equalities are allowed. No symmetry is inferred.

Consequently, to establish a universal lower bound for the first inverse weight under conditions depending only on the sector areas, it suffices to establish it on the union of these four attained core-saturated cases. Indeed every admissible body has an admissible saturated replacement whose target weight is no larger. In particular, any finite-data local minimum or any attained global body minimum must already have a core sector adjacent to EACH target endpoint; otherwise one can increase that endpoint slightly and strictly improve its objective.

All core constraints, the full PSD criterion, and every given cap/profile inequality must still be imposed in each case. The reduction does not by itself eliminate any of the four cases.

## 4. Extension to any finite arrangement of central lines

The same monotonicity applies to N>=2 distinct lines through zero. Choose fixed direction vectors e_i on their 2N cyclic rays, with e_(i+N)=-e_i, and write P_i=R_i e_i. Let

    d_i=det(e_i,e_(i+1))>0,
    c_i=det(e_(i-1),e_(i+1))/(d_(i-1)d_i).

Here c_i>=0. To see this, the consecutive angular gaps repeat after pi. Any two adjacent gaps have sum at most pi; for N=2 it is exactly pi, and for N>=3 it is strictly smaller. Thus the next-neighbor determinant is nonnegative.

The PSD matrix now has entries

    L_ii=1/(2W_(i-1))+1/(2W_i)-c_i/R_i^2,
    L_(i,i+1)=1/(2W_i)-1/(d_i R_i R_(i+1)).                 (8)

The same proof works because increasing R_i again raises the changed entries, and the allowable upper bound is

    R_i'<=min{2W_(i-1)/(d_(i-1)R_(i-1)),
              2W_i/(d_i R_(i+1))}.                        (9)

Opposite endpoints are nonadjacent, including when N=2, and can be saturated independently. All fixed-line cap areas and central sections other than the changed chord remain unchanged. The exact polygonal realization uses at most 4N vertices.

This is still a planar ordinary-body theorem. It does not assert a higher-dimensional section replacement or a mixed-integer interpolation rule.

## 5. Exact restrictions when unique sectors are saturated

Suppose every canonical cap has area at most `c k`, where `k` is total area and `c<1/2`. Set `epsilon=1-2c>0`. The actual sector identities give, for every permutation `(i,j,l)` of `(1,2,3)`,

    X_i-Y_i=k-q_j-q_l>=epsilon k.                       (10)

In particular all three unique sectors cannot simultaneously equal their core areas. Indeed their core-area product is

    (Ar/2)(Bt/2)(ab/2)=(at/2)(br/2)(AB/2),

the product of the opposite three core areas. If all unique sectors were cores, (10) and the double-sector core lower bounds would make the left product strictly larger than the right product, a contradiction.

For the both-unique saturated case `X_2=Bt/2,X_3=ab/2`, (10) gives the quantitative inequalities

    Bt>=br+2epsilon k,
    ab>=AB+2epsilon k.                                  (11)

Thus `r/t<B/b<a/A`, and in particular `at>Ar`. Multiplying the two inequalities in (11), then dividing by `Bb>0`, yields

    at-Ar>=2epsilon k(A/b+r/B)
                     +4epsilon^2 k^2/(Bb).              (12)

Since `Y_1>=at/2`, applying (10) also to `i=1` proves the actual lower bound on the remaining unique-sector excess,

    X_1-Ar/2>=epsilon k(1+A/b+r/B)
                      +2epsilon^2 k^2/(Bb).              (13)

This is a joint restriction on a single common body, not a freely assigned area row. It can be combined with the remaining PSD block or with any valid upper envelope for that same sector. It does not by itself eliminate the both-unique case. The one-unique saturated cases retain the corresponding one of (11); their other inequalities must not be inferred without the second saturation.
